sentences.text: The X was under the old rose bush.
Iris waited until Grandmother Rose was asleep.

She was not sure why she waited — Grandmother Rose would probably have come with her — but she felt that this was something she needed to do quietly, on her own, at night, when the butterflies could see her doing it.
She took the small trowel from the greenhouse.
She went out into the garden.
The moon was bright.
The old rose bush was enormous, and the ground under it was hard from years of roots.
Iris dug for a long time.
Her trowel hit something metal.
It was a small tin box, rust-red with age.
Iris pulled it up, brushed off the earth, and pried open the lid.
Inside was a compass.
It was a very old compass — brass, dented, with a needle that pointed in a wobbly, uncertain way.
Iris held it flat and watched the needle.
It swung.
It did not settle on north.
It kept moving.
She rotated it.
She held it still.
She held her breath.
The needle turned, and turned, and finally stopped.
It was not pointing north or south or east or west.
It was pointing straight up.
Iris frowned.
She tilted the compass.
She tapped it.
The needle wobbled a little, but it kept pointing up.
"Compasses don't point up," she whispered.
The garden did not answer.
She looked at the sky.
There were more stars than usual, because the village had no streetlights.
Iris held the compass toward the sky and turned very slowly in a circle.
The needle stayed pointing up, but as she turned, it seemed to be pointing at one particular part of the sky.
A star.
A star Iris did not know the name of, a small red one, low in the east.
She stared at it.
It stared back.
Behind her, in the greenhouse, the silver butterfly had opened its wings and closed them again, three times, very slowly, as if it were saying: yes.
That's the one.
